title: US forces capture Venezuela’s Maduro after strikes on Caracas
dek: President Trump said Nicolás Maduro and his wife were seized and flown out of the country to face criminal charges in New York.
body: The United States carried out air strikes on military sites in and around Venezuela’s capital, Caracas, early on 3 January. President Donald Trump then announced that US forces had captured President Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, and flown them out of the country. US officials said no American service members were killed in the operation.

The raid marked a dramatic escalation after months of US pressure on Maduro’s government, which Washington accuses of links to drug trafficking. Venezuela’s government declared a national emergency and condemned the action as military aggression. Legal experts questioned what authority the US relied on and whether Congress was consulted beforehand.

Maduro and his wife appeared in a federal court in Manhattan on 5 January and pleaded not guilty to charges including narco-terrorism, drug trafficking and weapons offences. Vice-President Delcy Rodríguez took over as interim leader in Caracas. The move raised wide questions about Venezuela’s future and the region’s stability.

title: Nvidia says its next Rubin AI chips are already in full production
dek: At CES in Las Vegas, chief executive Jensen Huang used his keynote to focus on data-centre computing and robotics rather than gaming graphics cards.
body: Nvidia used its keynote before the CES trade show in Las Vegas to say that Vera Rubin, its next generation of AI computing hardware, is now in full production. The platform is built from six new chips, including a Vera processor and a Rubin graphics processor, and partner systems are expected to reach customers in the second half of 2026.

Nvidia’s chips power much of the world’s AI training and use, so its product timing shapes spending plans at cloud providers and AI labs. The company claims Rubin can run AI models several times faster than its current Blackwell chips and cut the cost of each unit of AI output, though those figures come from Nvidia itself.

The presentation also covered self-driving car software and what Nvidia calls physical AI, meaning robots and machines that act in the real world. Notably, the company did not unveil a new consumer graphics card. Investors will watch whether customers take delivery of Rubin systems on the timetable Nvidia has set out.

title: Trump orders US exit from 66 international bodies, including the UN climate treaty
dek: The list covers the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change and the IPCC, the scientific panel that assesses climate research.
body: President Donald Trump signed a directive ordering US government agencies to stop taking part in and funding 66 international organisations, 31 of them linked to the United Nations. They include the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, the treaty behind yearly climate summits, and the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change. The White House said the groups put global agendas ahead of US priorities.

The United States is the world’s largest economy and one of the biggest emitters of greenhouse gases, so its absence weakens international cooperation on climate and other shared problems. The step goes beyond the earlier US exit from the Paris Agreement, because the UN climate treaty is the framework on which that deal rests.

UN climate chief Simon Stiell called the decision a serious own goal for the US, and European officials expressed regret. Legal experts have debated how and when a treaty withdrawal takes effect. Other governments now face pressure to fill funding gaps left by Washington at a range of global agencies.

title: Indonesia and Malaysia become the first countries to block Grok over deepfakes
dek: Regulators acted after Elon Musk’s AI chatbot was used to make sexualised fake images of real people, including women and minors.
body: Indonesia temporarily blocked access to Grok, the AI chatbot made by Elon Musk’s company xAI, and Malaysia followed a day later. Both governments acted after the tool’s image features were widely used to create sexually explicit, non-consensual edits of real photos. Malaysia’s communications regulator said access would stay blocked until effective safeguards were in place.

The two countries were the first to take such direct action, showing how Southeast Asian governments are willing to restrict global tech platforms over online harms. Indonesia’s communications minister described non-consensual sexual deepfakes as a serious violation of human rights and of people’s safety online.

Regulators in Europe, Britain, India and elsewhere also raised concerns about the images. xAI responded by limiting Grok’s image creation and editing tools to paying subscribers. The episode added to a wider global debate over how to hold AI companies responsible for content their tools produce.

title: Apple picks Google’s Gemini to power the next version of Siri
dek: The two rivals announced a multi-year deal under which Google’s AI models will underpin Apple’s own foundation models and a more personal Siri.
body: Apple and Google said in a joint statement that Apple’s next generation of AI models will be based on Google’s Gemini technology and cloud infrastructure. The multi-year arrangement is meant to power a more personalised Siri expected later in 2026, along with other Apple Intelligence features. Neither company disclosed the financial terms.

Apple has struggled to keep pace with rivals in generative AI, and its upgraded Siri had been delayed. Apple said it chose Google after evaluating the options and judging Gemini the strongest base. The deal also deepens ties between two companies that already have a long-running search partnership, which has drawn regulatory scrutiny.

Apple said its AI features will keep running on its devices and its own Private Cloud Compute servers, and that its privacy standards will not change. The deal does not replace Apple’s existing ChatGPT integration. Critics, including Elon Musk, argued it gives Google too much power, since it also controls Android and Chrome.

title: 2025 ranked as the planet’s third-hottest year on record
dek: Europe’s Copernicus service said the last three years together averaged more than 1.5C above pre-industrial levels for the first time.
body: The European Union’s Copernicus Climate Change Service said 2025 was the third-warmest year in its records, only marginally cooler than 2023 and behind 2024, the hottest. Global surface air temperature last year averaged about 1.47C above pre-industrial levels. Antarctica had its warmest year on record, while the Arctic had its second warmest.

For the first time, the average over a three-year period, 2023 to 2025, was above 1.5C, the limit that countries aimed to stay within under the Paris Agreement. That target is judged over decades rather than single years, but scientists say the world is getting very close to breaching it for good.

US group Berkeley Earth released similar findings the same day. Copernicus noted that a developing El Niño, a natural warming pattern in the Pacific, could make 2026 another record year. Scientists say each fraction of a degree of extra warming raises the risk of severe heatwaves and floods.

title: TSMC posts 35% jump in quarterly profit and plans record investment
dek: The world’s largest contract chipmaker said it will spend up to US$56 billion in 2026 as demand for AI chips keeps rising.
body: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co reported net profit of about NT$506 billion, roughly US$16 billion, for the October to December quarter, up 35 per cent from a year earlier and ahead of analysts’ estimates. Revenue rose 21 per cent. The company also said it will raise capital spending to between US$52 billion and US$56 billion this year, up from about US$40 billion in 2025.

TSMC makes advanced chips for companies such as Nvidia and Apple, so its results are a key gauge of the AI boom. A sharp rise in spending signals that it expects strong demand to continue, and it matters for suppliers across Asia, including equipment makers and firms in Singapore’s semiconductor supply chain.

Most of the new budget will go to the most advanced manufacturing processes. TSMC guided first-quarter revenue of roughly US$34.6 billion to US$35.8 billion. The company continues to expand outside Taiwan, including in Arizona, amid pressure from Washington to make more chips in the United States.

title: PM Wong removes Pritam Singh as Leader of the Opposition
dek: The move came a day after Parliament voted that the Workers’ Party chief was unsuitable for the role following his conviction.
body: Prime Minister Lawrence Wong removed Workers’ Party secretary-general Pritam Singh as Leader of the Opposition with immediate effect. The decision followed a parliamentary motion on 14 January, backed by PAP and Nominated MPs and opposed by the Workers’ Party MPs present, which found him unsuitable for the role. Singh’s conviction for lying to a parliamentary committee had been upheld on appeal in December.

It was the first time a Leader of the Opposition has been removed in Singapore. The post is not set out in the Constitution and is designated by the Prime Minister. It brings extra speaking time, the right to reply first in debates and a higher allowance. Singh remains an elected MP for Aljunied.

Mr Wong invited the Workers’ Party to nominate another elected MP for the role, as long as that person was not implicated in the earlier committee findings. The party said it would consider the matter through its internal processes and respond in due course. The episode is a significant moment for opposition politics in Singapore.

title: OpenAI to begin testing ads inside ChatGPT for free and low-cost users
dek: Sponsored products will appear below some answers for adult users in the US on the free tier and the cheapest paid plan.
body: OpenAI said it will start testing advertising in ChatGPT in the coming weeks. The ads will be shown to logged-in adults in the United States who use the free version or the low-cost ChatGPT Go plan. They will appear below responses when a sponsored product or service is relevant to the conversation. Higher-tier and business plans will stay ad-free.

ChatGPT is one of the most widely used consumer apps in the world, but running it is very expensive. Advertising gives OpenAI a new way to earn money from the large share of users who do not pay, and it is part of a wider push to diversify revenue as the company considers a possible stock market listing.

OpenAI said ads will not change the answers ChatGPT gives and that conversations will stay private from advertisers. How well those promises hold up will be closely watched by regulators and users. The test also puts OpenAI in more direct competition with Google and Meta for digital advertising budgets.

title: Gold and silver plunge after Trump names Kevin Warsh to lead the Fed
dek: Precious metals fell sharply from record highs as the dollar strengthened on the news of the US central bank nomination.
body: Gold and silver prices tumbled after US President Donald Trump said he would nominate former Federal Reserve official Kevin Warsh to succeed Jerome Powell as chair of the central bank. Gold had topped US$5,000 an ounce for the first time days earlier. Spot gold fell around 9 to 11 per cent during the session, while silver dropped by close to 30 per cent.

Gold had surged on worries about geopolitical tensions, tariffs and the independence of the Fed. Traders saw Warsh as a credible and inflation-focused choice, which eased some of those fears and lifted the US dollar. A stronger dollar tends to weigh on metals priced in the currency, and investors also rushed to lock in profits.

Even after the fall, gold ended January well above where it began the year. The swing showed how crowded the precious metals trade had become. Warsh still needs to be confirmed by the US Senate, and markets will look for clues on how quickly he would move on interest rates.

title: SpaceX buys Elon Musk’s AI company xAI in a record-breaking deal
dek: The merger brings the maker of the Grok chatbot under the rocket company, with Musk pointing to plans for data centres in space.
body: Elon Musk announced that SpaceX has acquired xAI, the artificial intelligence company behind the Grok chatbot. Under the agreement, xAI becomes a wholly owned subsidiary of SpaceX. A person familiar with the deal valued SpaceX at about US$1 trillion and xAI at about US$250 billion, making it the largest merger on record by value.

The deal joins two of Musk’s private companies at a time when AI developers are spending huge sums on computing power. Musk has linked the combination to his idea of placing AI data centres in orbit, powered by solar energy. Experts say that plan faces major technical hurdles, including cooling and launch costs.

SpaceX is reported to be preparing a large public share offering this year that could value the combined company even higher. Bringing xAI inside SpaceX may help fund the AI firm’s heavy spending, but it also ties the rocket business more closely to the fortunes of a young and costly AI venture.

title: Data and legal software stocks slide after Anthropic launches a legal AI tool
dek: Shares in Thomson Reuters, RELX and Wolters Kluwer fell steeply as investors worried AI agents could cut demand for their services.
body: Shares in companies that sell legal information and software fell sharply after AI company Anthropic released a legal plug-in for Claude Cowork, its AI assistant for office work. The tool can help in-house lawyers review contracts, sort confidentiality agreements and handle compliance tasks. Thomson Reuters fell as much as 18 per cent, while RELX and Wolters Kluwer each dropped around 13 to 14 per cent.

The sell-off spread to other software and data stocks, reflecting fears that AI agents could replace some paid software licences and services. It showed how quickly investors are now reacting to new AI products, and how firms that once seemed safe because of their specialised data may face new competition.

Some analysts said the reaction was overdone, noting the tool does not replace the legal research databases at the core of these businesses. Thomson Reuters’ chief executive described the drop as driven by anxiety rather than fundamentals. Markets remained jittery in the following weeks over which companies win or lose from AI.

title: Milan Cortina Winter Olympics open with a ceremony spread across four sites
dek: The Games began at Milan’s San Siro stadium, with two cauldrons lit for an event hosted across a wide area of northern Italy.
body: The 2026 Winter Olympics opened in Italy on 6 February with a ceremony centred on Milan’s San Siro stadium. For the first time, the opening was held across four sites, and two Olympic cauldrons were lit to reflect the shared hosting. Former Italian ski stars Alberto Tomba and Deborah Compagnoni lit the cauldron at Milan’s Arco della Pace.

These Games are among the most spread-out in Olympic history, using existing venues across the Alps and northern Italy rather than building everything in one place. Organisers said the approach was meant to cut costs and environmental impact, a key concern as warmer winters reduce reliable snow.

Competition ran until 22 February, with the closing ceremony held in the ancient Roman arena in Verona. Singer Andrea Bocelli and pop star Mariah Carey were among the performers at the opening show. The ceremony set the tone for Games that organisers framed around the theme of harmony.

title: Japan’s ruling LDP wins a landslide in Takaichi’s snap election
dek: Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s party won more than 300 seats in the lower house, its best result since it was founded in 1955.
body: Japan’s Liberal Democratic Party won a sweeping victory in a snap general election held on 8 February. Public broadcaster NHK’s count gave the LDP alone 316 of the 465 seats in the House of Representatives, far above the number needed for a majority. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, the country’s first female leader, had called the vote early to take advantage of high approval ratings.

Together with its coalition partner, the Japan Innovation Party, the LDP now holds a two-thirds supermajority. That allows the government to override the upper house, where it lacks control, making it easier to pass its plans. The win gives Takaichi a strong mandate early in her time as leader.

Takaichi has promised tax cuts and higher defence spending aimed at countering China. Her spending plans have unsettled some investors in Japan’s bond market. The smaller anti-immigration party Sanseito was also expected to gain seats, reflecting a shift in Japanese politics.

title: Bad Bunny headlines the Super Bowl halftime show in Spanish
dek: The Puerto Rican star’s set at Super Bowl LX in California featured guest appearances from Lady Gaga and Ricky Martin.
body: Puerto Rican singer Bad Bunny performed the halftime show at Super Bowl LX at Levi’s Stadium in Santa Clara, California. His roughly 13-minute set was performed almost entirely in Spanish and opened in a staged sugar cane field, a nod to Puerto Rican farm workers. Lady Gaga and Ricky Martin joined him on stage as surprise guests.

The halftime show is one of the most-watched music performances in the world each year. Bad Bunny is the first reggaeton and Latin trap artist to headline it on his own, and his booking had drawn political debate in the US before the game. Reviewers described the show as a celebration of Latino culture and unity.

The staging featured scenes of everyday Puerto Rican life, from barbers to food stalls. Bad Bunny had previously appeared at the 2020 Super Bowl alongside Shakira and Jennifer Lopez. The show was produced by Roc Nation with Apple Music as the halftime partner.

title: Singapore Budget 2026 sets out national AI push and support for households
dek: Prime Minister Lawrence Wong announced a new National AI Council, cash payouts for adults and a corporate tax rebate for firms.
body: Prime Minister and Finance Minister Lawrence Wong delivered Singapore’s Budget 2026 in Parliament on 12 February. Total spending was put at about S$154.7 billion for the financial year. He announced national AI Missions in sectors such as advanced manufacturing, finance and healthcare, and a new National AI Council that he will chair himself.

Households will receive help with living costs, including cash payouts of S$200 to S$400 for eligible adults, extra U-Save rebates and S$500 in CDC vouchers for every Singaporean household in January 2027. Companies that employed at least one local worker will get a 40 per cent corporate income tax rebate for the 2026 assessment year, capped at S$30,000.

The economy grew about 5 per cent in 2025, better than expected, but growth is forecast to slow to between 2 and 4 per cent in 2026 amid global uncertainty. The Budget also raises qualifying salaries for some skilled foreign workers and levies in certain sectors. Parliament will debate the plans in the coming weeks.
source_name: The Straits Times (via Asia News Network)

title: US government repeals the scientific finding behind its climate rules
dek: The Environmental Protection Agency scrapped the 2009 endangerment finding and the greenhouse gas standards for vehicles that rested on it.
body: President Donald Trump and Environmental Protection Agency head Lee Zeldin announced the final repeal of the 2009 endangerment finding at a White House event. That finding said greenhouse gases endanger public health and welfare. The new rule also removes all federal greenhouse gas emission standards for cars, trucks and engines.

The finding has been the legal foundation for almost all US climate regulation under the Clean Air Act, covering vehicles, power plants and other polluters. Removing it makes it much harder for future officials to limit emissions without new laws from Congress. The administration said the change would save more than US$1.3 trillion, but did not estimate health or environmental costs.

Environmental groups and several states, including California, said they would challenge the repeal in court, and the case is widely expected to reach the Supreme Court. The rule was due to take effect in April. The move adds to a series of US steps away from climate commitments made under earlier governments.

title: Bangladesh’s BNP wins first election since the 2024 uprising
dek: The Bangladesh Nationalist Party secured a two-thirds majority, putting Tarique Rahman on course to become prime minister.
body: The Bangladesh Nationalist Party won a decisive victory in the general election held on 12 February. Official figures gave the BNP-led alliance more than 200 of the 300 seats, well above the 151 needed for a majority, while an alliance led by the Islamist party Jamaat-e-Islami came second. BNP leader Tarique Rahman was set to become prime minister.

It was the first national vote since mass protests in 2024 forced former prime minister Sheikh Hasina from power. Her Awami League party was barred from taking part. The result returns the BNP to government after a long time in opposition and marks a major turning point for the South Asian country.

Voters also approved, in a referendum held the same day, a package of political reforms known as the July Charter. Turnout was close to 60 per cent. The new government faces pressure to steady the economy, restore confidence in institutions and deliver the reforms that protesters demanded.

title: US Supreme Court strikes down Trump’s sweeping emergency tariffs
dek: In a 6-3 ruling, the justices said a national emergency law does not give the president power to impose import taxes.
body: The US Supreme Court ruled 6-3 that President Donald Trump did not have authority to impose broad tariffs under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act. The decision invalidated the so-called reciprocal tariffs on goods from almost every trading partner and the drug-related tariffs on Canada, Mexico and China. Chief Justice John Roberts wrote that the power to tax belongs to Congress.

Tariffs were a central part of Trump’s economic agenda and had reshaped trade talks with dozens of countries, including in Asia. The ruling raised the prospect of refunds for importers that had paid the duties. Tariffs imposed under other laws, such as those on steel and cars, were not affected.

Trump called the ruling deeply disappointing and quickly announced a temporary 10 per cent global tariff under a different law that limits such duties to 150 days. That replacement could also face legal challenges. US customs officials said they would stop collecting the struck-down tariffs from 24 February.

title: India’s AI summit ends with a non-binding declaration backed by 88 parties
dek: Countries including the US and China endorsed the New Delhi Declaration, which calls for the benefits of AI to be shared widely.
body: The India AI Impact Summit, held in New Delhi from 16 to 21 February, closed with the adoption of the New Delhi Declaration on AI Impact. Organisers said 88 countries and international organisations endorsed it, with signatories including the United States, Britain, Canada, China and Germany. The text is organised around seven themes, from skills to energy-efficient AI systems.

It was the first major global AI summit hosted in the Global South, and India used it to argue that developing countries should share in the gains from AI. Getting both Washington and Beijing to sign the same document is notable at a time of sharp rivalry between them over AI and chips.

The declaration is voluntary and sets out principles rather than rules. Critics said it offered few practical details and did not address how computing power, data and expertise remain concentrated in a handful of countries and companies. Future summits will show whether its goals turn into concrete programmes.

title: Apple unveils the MacBook Neo, its cheapest laptop yet at US$599
dek: The new 13-inch MacBook runs on an iPhone-class chip and is aimed at students and everyday users.
body: Apple announced the MacBook Neo on March 4, a 13-inch laptop starting at US$599 in the United States, with a lower price for education buyers. Pre-orders opened the same day and the machine went on sale on March 11. It uses the A18 Pro chip, from the same family that powers recent iPhones, and comes in four colours.

The Neo is the first time Apple has offered a Mac laptop at this price level, putting it in direct competition with Chromebooks and budget Windows machines. Using a phone chip helps Apple keep costs down, and the company is pitching the laptop at students and people who mostly browse, write and stream rather than edit video.

Apple says the Neo can run for up to 16 hours on a charge. A higher-priced version adds more storage and Touch ID. Analysts will be watching whether the cheaper entry point draws new customers into Apple’s ecosystem, especially in schools and price-sensitive markets where Windows and Chromebooks have long dominated.

title: China sets its lowest growth target in decades at 4.5% to 5%
dek: Premier Li Qiang unveiled the goal at the National People’s Congress as deflation and trade tensions weigh on the economy.
body: China set its 2026 economic growth target at 4.5% to 5%, Premier Li Qiang told the opening of the National People’s Congress in Beijing on March 5. It is the lowest goal since the early 1990s and a step down from the “around 5%” target used for the previous three years. The meeting also outlined the country’s 15th Five-Year Plan for 2026 to 2030.

The lower range reflects weak consumer demand, falling prices and pressure from tariffs on Chinese exports. Some analysts read it as a sign that Beijing is moving away from chasing headline numbers and putting more weight on the quality of growth, while giving policymakers room to respond to shocks from abroad.

The government kept its budget deficit goal at around 4% of GDP and aims to create 12 million urban jobs. Observers said the plan supports domestic spending but stops short of a large new stimulus package. Investors will watch upcoming data on retail sales and prices to judge whether the target is realistic.

title: Iran names Mojtaba Khamenei as supreme leader after his father’s killing
dek: The Assembly of Experts chose the late leader’s son about a week into the US-Israeli war on Iran.
body: Iran’s Assembly of Experts named Mojtaba Khamenei as the country’s new supreme leader on March 8. He replaces his father, Ali Khamenei, who was killed in US-Israeli strikes at the start of the war that began on February 28. He becomes only the third person to hold the post since the 1979 revolution.

The choice matters because the supreme leader has the final say on war, security and foreign policy. Analysts describe the younger Khamenei as more hardline than his father, and his rise depended heavily on backing from the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, which quickly pledged its loyalty. US President Donald Trump said he was disappointed by the decision.

The appointment came as fighting spread across the Gulf and oil prices surged. Reports said the new leader had been injured and was keeping out of public view. Some analysts expect him to be a transitional figure, but his early statements on keeping the Strait of Hormuz closed quickly moved global energy markets.

title: Oil closes above US$100 despite record release of emergency reserves
dek: Brent crude jumped after Iran said the Strait of Hormuz would stay shut, a day after IEA members agreed to free up 400 million barrels.
body: Brent crude closed at about US$100 a barrel on March 12, its first close above that level since August 2022, after Iran’s new supreme leader said the Strait of Hormuz must remain closed. The jump came a day after the International Energy Agency’s member countries agreed to release a record 400 million barrels from emergency stockpiles.

Roughly a fifth of the world’s oil normally passes through the strait, so its closure is a major supply shock. The IEA release is more than double the previous record set in 2022, but analysts said it could cover only part of the shortfall, which is why prices kept rising after the announcement.

The United States pledged 172 million barrels from its Strategic Petroleum Reserve, with deliveries expected to take months. Each country sets its own release pace. Prices remained volatile through March, swinging sharply on news about the war, and higher fuel costs began to feed into inflation worries for central banks around the world.

title: Nvidia expects US$1 trillion in orders for its Blackwell and Vera Rubin chips
dek: At its annual GTC conference, the chipmaker also showed new AI agent software, self-driving partners and a chip system for space.
body: Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang told the company’s GTC conference in San Jose on March 16 that he expects orders for its Blackwell and Vera Rubin chips to reach US$1 trillion through 2027. That is double the US$500 billion opportunity he described a year earlier. He also said Vera Rubin systems will roll out later this year.

The forecast signals that spending on AI data centres is still climbing fast, which matters for chip suppliers across Asia, including Taiwan and South Korea. Nvidia also unveiled NemoClaw, a platform for businesses to run AI agents, and added Hyundai, Nissan, BYD and Geely to its list of self-driving technology partners.

Other announcements included a new inference chip based on technology from startup Groq and a Vera Rubin module for satellites and orbital computing. Investors gave a mixed response: Nvidia’s shares rose modestly on the day but gave up part of their early gains, suggesting Wall Street wants proof that demand will hold up.

title: US Federal Reserve holds rates steady as oil shock lifts inflation forecasts
dek: Policymakers kept the benchmark rate at 3.5% to 3.75% and still pencilled in one cut for 2026.
body: The US Federal Reserve left its benchmark interest rate unchanged in a range of 3.5% to 3.75% on March 18. The vote was 11 to 1, with Governor Stephen Miran preferring a cut. Fed officials raised their forecast for inflation this year, citing the sharp jump in oil prices caused by the war in the Middle East.

US rates influence borrowing costs and currency moves worldwide, including in Singapore and the wider region. Chair Jerome Powell said short-term inflation expectations had risen with energy prices, but the Fed broadly expected the disruption to be temporary. Its projections still showed one rate cut in 2026, though fewer officials now expect two.

Powell admitted the outlook was highly uncertain and that the Fed did not yet know how the conflict would play out. Later in March he said the central bank saw no need to raise rates because of the oil shock, but some officials warned that a hike could come back on the table if prices stayed high.

title: Singapore and Japan upgrade ties to a strategic partnership
dek: Prime Minister Lawrence Wong’s visit to Tokyo marked 60 years of diplomatic relations between the two countries.
body: Prime Minister Lawrence Wong and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi announced on March 18 that Singapore and Japan would raise their relationship to a strategic partnership. The move came during Mr Wong’s first official visit to Japan as prime minister, from March 17 to 19, which marked the 60th anniversary of diplomatic ties.

The new framework covers five areas: trade, technology, security and defence, green energy, and wider partnerships. Japan is one of Singapore’s major investors, and both sides want closer work on artificial intelligence, semiconductors and maritime security as global supply chains and regional tensions shift.

Planned follow-ups include a space cooperation agreement between Japan’s space agency JAXA and Singapore’s National Space Agency, and a new dialogue on digital policy. As ASEAN’s coordinator for relations with Japan, Singapore also pledged to support regional projects such as the ASEAN Power Grid.

title: Trump cites Pearl Harbor in Oval Office talks with Japan’s Takaichi
dek: The summit, meant to focus on trade, was dominated by the Iran war and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
body: Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi met US President Donald Trump at the White House on March 19. Asked why allies were not warned before the February 28 strikes on Iran, Mr Trump referred to the 1941 Pearl Harbor attack, saying Japan understood surprise. The remark drew visible unease from Ms Takaichi and debate back home.

Japan relies heavily on Middle East oil that passes through the Strait of Hormuz, so the war is a direct economic threat. Ms Takaichi condemned Iran’s actions, while Mr Trump praised Japan’s support. Her office said Washington had made no specific request for Japan to send ships to the region.

The two leaders were also expected to advance deals under Japan’s pledge of US$550 billion in US investment, made in return for lower tariffs. Analysts said Tokyo came away with economic gains, though some Japanese commentators criticised the prime minister for not pushing back on the Pearl Harbor comment.

title: BTS returns with a free comeback concert in central Seoul
dek: The K-pop group played Gwanghwamun Square after releasing its album Arirang, its first full return in years.
body: BTS staged a free, hour-long outdoor concert in Seoul’s Gwanghwamun Square on March 21, a day after releasing its new album, Arirang. It was the group’s first major show together in years, following a long break while its members completed South Korea’s mandatory military service. Netflix streamed the performance live around the world.

BTS is one of South Korea’s biggest cultural exports, and its return was closely watched by fans, the music industry and the government, which sees K-pop as a key part of the country’s soft power. Central Seoul was largely closed off for the event, though crowd estimates varied widely and fell short of official forecasts.

The smaller-than-expected turnout weighed on shares of Hybe, the group’s management company, which fell sharply the following Monday. Attention now turns to a world tour starting in April, which is set to run into 2027 and is expected to be one of the largest concert tours of the year.

title: UN weather agency says the past 11 years were the hottest on record
dek: The WMO’s annual climate report also found Earth is trapping more heat than at any point since measurements began.
body: The World Meteorological Organization released its State of the Global Climate 2025 report on March 23. It found that 2015 to 2025 were the 11 warmest years on record, with 2025 ranking second or third at about 1.43°C above pre-industrial levels. Greenhouse gas concentrations and ocean heat content both hit new highs.

For the first time, the report tracked Earth’s energy imbalance, the gap between heat coming in and heat escaping to space, which reached its highest level since records began in 1960. That extra heat drives rising seas, melting ice and harsher extremes, which affect low-lying, tropical cities such as Singapore.

The report also noted near-record low Arctic sea ice and heavy glacier losses. UN Secretary-General António Guterres described the climate as being in a state of emergency. The findings add pressure on governments to strengthen their emissions plans ahead of the next round of UN climate talks later in the year.

title: Artemis II launches four astronauts on the first crewed Moon trip since 1972
dek: NASA’s mission flew around the Moon and back over about ten days, testing the Orion spacecraft with people on board.
body: NASA launched the Artemis II mission from Kennedy Space Center in Florida on April 1. The crew of Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Canadian astronaut Jeremy Hansen rode the Space Launch System rocket and Orion capsule on a path that looped around the Moon without landing, before splashing down in the Pacific on April 10.

It was the first time humans had travelled beyond low Earth orbit in more than 50 years, and the first crewed trip to the Moon’s vicinity since Apollo 17. The flight was designed to prove that Orion’s life support, navigation and heat shield work safely with astronauts on board.

The mission is a stepping stone to a planned crewed lunar landing later in the Artemis programme. NASA will study data from the flight before committing to that next step. The United States is racing China, which has its own plans to land astronauts on the Moon by the end of the decade.

title: US and Iran agree to a two-week ceasefire brokered by Pakistan
dek: The truce was tied to reopening the Strait of Hormuz, though talks in Islamabad later ended without a deal.
body: US President Donald Trump announced a two-week ceasefire with Iran on April 7, after Pakistan’s prime minister asked him to delay planned strikes on Iranian infrastructure. The pause depended on Iran reopening the Strait of Hormuz. Iran accepted on condition that US and Israeli attacks stopped, and its supreme leader ordered forces to cease firing.

The truce offered the first real pause in a war that began on February 28 and had choked global oil and gas shipments. However, the deal’s scope was disputed: Israel said it did not cover fighting with Hezbollah in Lebanon, and Gulf states reported attacks within hours of the announcement.

Face-to-face talks in Islamabad, led on the US side by Vice President JD Vance, ended on April 12 without agreement. As the deadline approached on April 21, Mr Trump extended the ceasefire without setting an end date, while Iranian officials dismissed the move and did not send a delegation back to Pakistan.

title: Hungary’s Viktor Orbán concedes defeat to Péter Magyar after 16 years
dek: Magyar’s Tisza party won a two-thirds majority in a record-turnout election, a result welcomed by EU leaders.
body: Péter Magyar’s Tisza party won Hungary’s parliamentary election on April 12, ending Viktor Orbán’s 16 years as prime minister. Early official results gave Tisza a two-thirds majority in the 199-seat parliament, enough to change the constitution. Turnout was a record of around 79%. Mr Orbán conceded, calling the result painful but clear.

Mr Orbán had often clashed with the European Union and kept close ties with Russia, and he had been endorsed by US President Donald Trump. EU leaders welcomed the outcome, and analysts said it could unlock a large EU loan for Ukraine that Budapest had been blocking.

Mr Magyar, a former insider in Mr Orbán’s Fidesz party, is expected to try to reverse some of the constitutional and media changes made under his predecessor. Fidesz will now sit in opposition. Russia said it would seek practical ties with the new government, while Brussels looks for quick moves on rule-of-law concerns.

title: Rory McIlroy wins a second straight Masters title
dek: The Northern Irishman beat Scottie Scheffler by one shot to become the first back-to-back champion since Tiger Woods.
body: Rory McIlroy won the Masters at Augusta National on April 12, finishing at 12 under par and one stroke ahead of Scottie Scheffler. He had built a record six-shot lead after two rounds but lost it over the weekend, before fighting back on the final day to claim the green jacket again.

The win makes McIlroy only the fourth player to win consecutive Masters titles, joining Jack Nicklaus, Nick Faldo and Tiger Woods, who last did it in 2001 and 2002. It cements his place among the leading golfers of his generation after years in which major titles had proved elusive.

McIlroy’s victory came a year after he completed golf’s career grand slam at Augusta. His duel with world number one Scheffler is shaping up as the main rivalry of the season, with the PGA Championship, US Open and Open Championship still to come later in the year.

title: MAS tightens monetary policy as energy costs raise inflation risks
dek: Singapore’s central bank slightly increased the pace at which the Singapore dollar is allowed to strengthen.
body: The Monetary Authority of Singapore said on April 14 it would slightly increase the rate at which the Singapore dollar is allowed to rise against a basket of trading partners’ currencies. The width and centre of the policy band were left unchanged. MAS also raised its 2026 forecast for core and headline inflation to 1.5% to 2.5%.

Singapore manages monetary policy through its exchange rate rather than interest rates. A stronger currency makes imports cheaper, which helps offset the jump in global energy prices caused by the Middle East war. Most economists polled ahead of the decision had expected some tightening.

MAS said the economy grew 4.6% year on year in the first quarter, though momentum slowed from the previous quarter. The move came a week after the government announced close to S$1 billion in extra support for households and businesses to cope with higher costs. MAS’s next scheduled policy review is in July.

title: TSMC posts record quarterly profit, up 58% on AI chip demand
dek: The world’s largest contract chipmaker beat forecasts as orders for artificial intelligence processors kept growing.
body: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co reported on April 16 that first-quarter net profit rose 58% from a year earlier to a record NT$572.5 billion, beating analyst estimates. Revenue climbed about 35% to NT$1.13 trillion, and gross margin came in at 66.2%, above the top of the company’s own guidance.

TSMC makes advanced chips for Nvidia, Apple and many other firms, so its results are a key gauge of the global AI boom. Chief executive C.C. Wei described AI-related demand as extremely robust, easing some investor worries that spending on data centres might slow amid the oil shock and wider economic uncertainty.

The company forecast second-quarter revenue of roughly US$39 billion to US$40 billion, pointing to further growth. TSMC continues to expand production in Taiwan, the United States and Japan, as customers and governments push to secure supplies of the most advanced chips and reduce reliance on a single location.

title: Tim Cook to step down as Apple CEO, with John Ternus taking over
dek: Apple’s hardware engineering chief will become chief executive on September 1, while Cook moves to executive chairman.
body: Apple announced on April 20 that Tim Cook will step down as chief executive and become executive chairman of the board. He will be succeeded by John Ternus, the company’s senior vice-president of hardware engineering, with the change taking effect on September 1. Mr Cook has led Apple since 2011, taking over from co-founder Steve Jobs.

Mr Cook’s tenure saw Apple grow into one of the world’s most valuable companies, expanding services and moving Macs to its own chips. Mr Ternus, an engineer who joined Apple in 2001, inherits the task of keeping the company competitive as artificial intelligence reshapes the technology industry.

Apple described the handover as part of a long-planned succession approved unanimously by its board. Mr Ternus will also join the board. Observers expect him to focus on hardware and on catching up in AI, an area where Apple has been seen as trailing rivals such as Google, Microsoft and OpenAI.

title: Clean power met all new global electricity demand in 2025, Ember finds
dek: Solar and wind covered the growth in power use, while China and India both cut fossil-fuel generation.
body: Low-emission sources such as solar, wind, hydro and nuclear met all of the growth in global electricity demand in 2025, according to a report by energy think tank Ember published on April 21. It was the first time this has happened, leaving no room for fossil-fuel power to increase. Solar alone covered about three-quarters of the new demand.

Clean sources supplied a record 42.6% of the world’s electricity. China and India together reduced fossil-fuel generation for the first time this century, a significant shift because they are among the largest users of coal. Ember sees 2025 as a turning point and expects fossil power’s share to keep falling.

Other analysts urged caution, noting that demand growth in 2025 was fairly ordinary and that the trend must hold through extreme heat and cold. Fossil fuels still produce most of the world’s power, and experts say faster progress on storage and grids is needed to meet global warming goals.

title: OpenAI releases GPT-5.5, pitching it as stronger at coding and research
dek: The new model rolled out first to paying ChatGPT and Codex users, with developer access promised later.
body: OpenAI launched GPT-5.5 on April 23, its newest artificial intelligence model and the successor to GPT-5.4. It was made available to paying ChatGPT subscribers on the Plus, Pro, Business and Enterprise plans, as well as in the Codex coding tool. OpenAI said access for developers through its API would follow soon.

The company said the model is faster and more efficient than its predecessor and performs better on coding, computer use and in-depth research tasks. It claimed GPT-5.5 beat competing models from Google and Anthropic on its published benchmarks, as the race to build AI agents that can complete tasks on their own intensifies.

OpenAI rated the model as high risk, though below its critical threshold, for cybersecurity capabilities, and said wider deployment needed extra safeguards. Commentators saw the release as another step towards the company’s goal of a single “super app” combining chat, coding, browsing and other tools.

title: ICC commits former Philippine president Duterte to trial over drug war killings
dek: Judges confirmed three counts of murder as crimes against humanity, though no trial date has been set.
body: Judges at the International Criminal Court in The Hague confirmed three counts of murder as crimes against humanity against former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte on April 23 and sent the case to trial. The charges relate to killings during his anti-drug campaign. A day earlier, appeals judges rejected his lawyers’ argument that the court had no jurisdiction.

The decision is a milestone for the ICC and for families of victims of the drug war, which human rights groups say killed thousands of people while Mr Duterte was president from 2016 to 2022. Official police figures put the toll far lower than rights groups’ estimates.

Mr Duterte, who was arrested and flown to The Hague in 2025, denies the charges, and his defence says he is not mentally fit to follow proceedings. No start date has been announced, and the court has previously taken up to a year to move from confirming charges to opening a trial.

title: Singapore to merge its skills and jobs agencies as PM Wong addresses AI disruption
dek: At the May Day Rally, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said the government cannot save every job but will stand behind every worker as AI reshapes the economy.
body: Prime Minister Lawrence Wong used his May Day Rally speech on 1 May to set out how Singapore plans to handle job changes driven by artificial intelligence. He announced that SkillsFuture Singapore and Workforce Singapore will be combined into a new Skills and Workforce Development Agency, overseen jointly by the Ministry of Manpower and the Ministry of Education.

Bringing training and job matching under one roof is meant to make it easier for workers to retrain and move into new roles as AI changes how companies operate. Mr Wong said some jobs would change or disappear, and that the government's promise is to protect workers rather than every individual position.

He also backed the new Tripartite Jobs Council formed by NTUC, the manpower ministry and employers, and called for company training committees to be scaled up sector by sector. The speech came against a tougher backdrop, with Mr Wong warning that conflict in the Middle East was pushing up energy costs and could slow growth.

title: AI chipmaker Cerebras raises $5.5bn in the year's biggest US tech listing so far
dek: Shares in the Nvidia rival more than doubled at the open on their first day of trading before settling well above the offer price.
body: Cerebras Systems, which designs very large chips built specifically for artificial intelligence, priced its initial public offering at US$185 a share and raised about US$5.5 billion. The price was well above the range the company first set. When trading began on 14 May, the stock opened at US$385 and closed at about US$311.

The listing showed how hungry investors remain for companies tied to the AI boom, especially those seen as challengers to Nvidia. Cerebras is pitching its hardware for inference, the computing work done when AI models answer users' questions, and counts OpenAI, Amazon Web Services and the UAE's G42 among its customers.

TechCrunch described the deal as the start of a busy season for tech listings in 2026. Closing-day figures put the company's value at roughly US$66 billion. The strong debut was widely watched as a signal for other large private technology firms weighing whether to go public.

title: Trump claims big trade wins after Beijing summit, but China confirms few details
dek: The US president said China would buy Boeing jets and American soybeans, while Beijing spoke only in general terms about stable trade ties.
body: US President Donald Trump wrapped up a two-day summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Beijing saying the two sides had reached trade deals that were good for both countries. He said China had agreed to buy 200 Boeing aircraft, possibly with more to follow, along with billions of dollars of American soybeans.

China's foreign ministry did not confirm any new purchase deals, saying only that both countries had agreed to keep trade stable and widen cooperation. The two sides did agree to set up a Board of Trade to manage commercial ties. Markets and businesses had hoped the meeting would ease years of tension between the world's two largest economies.

US officials cautioned that much work remained before the announcements would take effect. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said agricultural purchase arrangements had been firmed up. Mr Trump said tariffs were not discussed, and Mr Xi warned that Taiwan remains the most sensitive issue in the relationship.

title: NextEra agrees to buy Dominion Energy in a $67bn all-stock utility deal
dek: The merger would create one of the world's largest regulated electricity companies as US power demand from data centres climbs.
body: NextEra Energy, the parent of Florida Power & Light, agreed to acquire Virginia-based Dominion Energy in an all-stock deal worth about US$67 billion. Dominion shareholders would receive 0.8138 NextEra shares for each share they own and would hold roughly a quarter of the combined company, which would serve about 10 million customers.

The deal is one of the largest utility mergers on record and is closely tied to soaring electricity demand from AI data centres, many of which are clustered in Dominion's Virginia territory. Combining the two firms would give NextEra a dominant position in a region that is struggling to keep up with rising power use.

Both boards have approved the merger, but it still needs shareholder votes and federal and state regulatory approval. The companies expect it to close in 12 to 18 months and have proposed about US$2.25 billion in bill credits for Dominion customers in Virginia and the Carolinas over two years after completion.

title: Google makes Gemini 3.5 Flash its default AI model and bets on agents
dek: At its I/O developer conference, Google said the new model now powers the Gemini app and AI Mode in Search worldwide.
body: Google opened its annual I/O conference on 19 May by launching Gemini 3.5 Flash, a model it says is its strongest yet for coding and for agents that carry out tasks on their own. It became the default model in the Gemini app and in AI Mode in Search globally, and is available to developers through Google's tools and API.

The launch marks a shift in emphasis from chatbots that answer questions to software that acts for users. Google also unveiled Gemini Spark, a personal agent meant to run around the clock to help manage people's digital lives, and said users will be able to build and manage their own agents inside Search.

A more powerful Gemini 3.5 Pro model is still to come, and Google said it will work alongside Flash, planning tasks while Flash handles the individual steps. The company also said the new models carry stronger safeguards against misuse in areas such as cyber attacks and dangerous weapons.

title: Putin and Xi sign dozens of agreements in Beijing but leave gas pipeline unresolved
dek: The Russian leader's visit came a week after Donald Trump's trip to China, but the long-discussed Power of Siberia 2 pipeline still has no start date.
body: Russian President Vladimir Putin held talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Beijing on 20 May during a two-day visit. The two leaders oversaw the signing of around 40 documents, including a joint declaration on what they called a multipolar world and a lengthy statement on deepening their strategic partnership.

The visit was closely watched because China hosted the leaders of both Russia and the United States within the same month. Energy was high on the agenda, but the two sides failed to settle the timing or gas price for the Power of Siberia 2 pipeline, a project Moscow sees as vital for selling gas to Asia.

The Kremlin said only basic parameters for the pipeline's route and construction had been agreed. The trip marked 25 years since the two countries signed their friendship treaty. Their joint statement also restated shared positions on Taiwan and Ukraine and criticised the planned US Golden Dome missile defence system.

title: Meta begins cutting about 8,000 jobs as it reorganises around AI
dek: The layoffs, about a tenth of the workforce, started on 20 May, with thousands of other staff moved into new AI-focused teams.
body: Meta began laying off roughly 8,000 employees on 20 May, about 10 per cent of its workforce, in a restructuring first flagged in an internal memo in April. The company also dropped plans to fill around 6,000 open positions, and moved about 7,000 existing staff into newly created teams focused on building AI tools and apps.

The cuts are one of the clearest examples of a large tech company reshaping its workforce to pay for heavy spending on artificial intelligence. In a memo to staff, chief executive Mark Zuckerberg argued that success in the fiercely competitive AI race is not guaranteed, and said the company needed to become leaner.

Affected US employees were offered 16 weeks of base severance pay plus two more weeks for each year of service. Meta said the changes were part of an ongoing effort to run the company more efficiently. The cuts came alongside similar moves at other tech firms that have cited AI in decisions to shrink staff.

title: Singapore commits S$350m to research on living longer and healthier lives
dek: The five-year national challenge will fund work on brain health and physical decline as the country's population ages quickly.
body: Health Minister Ong Ye Kung announced on 22 May a S$350 million research programme called the Grand Challenge on Maximising Healthy and Successful Longevity. It will focus on three areas: brain health, physical function, and new social and environmental approaches that help older people stay well. Priorities include vascular dementia and the loss of muscle strength that often comes with age.

Singapore is ageing fast, and by 2030 about one in four residents is expected to be 65 or older. Mr Ong said the goal is not only to help people live longer but to help them live well, narrowing the gap of around a decade between Singaporeans' total lifespan and the years they spend in good health.

The programme sits under the national research and innovation plan and is open to researchers, public institutions and companies working in partnership. It was announced at the National Medical Research Council's annual awards event. Details of the first funded projects have not yet been released.

title: Romanian director Cristian Mungiu wins his second Palme d'Or at Cannes with Fjord
dek: The jury, led by South Korean filmmaker Park Chan-wook, also gave Barbra Streisand an honorary award at the 79th festival.
body: The Cannes Film Festival ended on 23 May with its top prize, the Palme d'Or, going to Fjord, a drama by Romanian director Cristian Mungiu starring Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve. The jury was led by South Korean director Park Chan-wook. The runner-up Grand Prix went to Minotaur by Russian filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev.

The win makes Mungiu only the tenth director to take the Palme d'Or twice. His first came in 2007 for 4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days, a landmark of the Romanian new wave. A Cannes win usually gives a film a major boost with distributors and in the awards season that follows.

Both acting prizes were shared this year. Virginie Efira and Tao Okamoto won best actress for All of a Sudden, while Emmanuel Macchia and Valentin Campagne shared best actor for Coward. The best director award was also split, and Barbra Streisand received an honorary Palme d'Or.

title: Hegseth urges Asian allies to spend more on defence but softens tone on China
dek: Speaking at the Shangri-La Dialogue in Singapore, the US defence secretary said ties with Beijing were better than in years.
body: US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth used his speech at the Shangri-La Dialogue in Singapore on 30 May to press Asian partners to raise military spending in response to China's large military build-up. At the same time, he said relations between Washington and Beijing were better than they had been for many years.

The speech was noticeably milder than his address at the same forum a year earlier, when he sharply criticised China. It followed a Trump-Xi summit in Beijing that both sides called a success. Hegseth did not mention Taiwan in his remarks and, when asked, said future arms sales to the island were a matter for President Trump.

China again sent a lower-level delegation of military scholars rather than its defence minister. Some analysts in the audience said the speech offered little detail on how to manage tensions. On Iran, Hegseth said the US would not accept any deal that failed to stop Tehran from obtaining a nuclear weapon.

title: Nvidia unveils RTX Spark, its first chip for Windows laptops and desktops
dek: Microsoft, Dell, HP and others plan to ship PCs with the Arm-based chip this autumn, putting Nvidia in direct competition with Intel and AMD.
body: Nvidia used the opening of the Computex trade show in Taipei to launch RTX Spark, a chip that combines a processor and graphics on one piece of silicon for Windows PCs. The company says it delivers about one petaflop of AI computing power. Laptops using it are due this autumn from Asus, Dell, HP, Lenovo, Microsoft Surface and MSI.

The move takes Nvidia, best known for the graphics chips that power AI data centres, into the market for the main processors in personal computers, long led by Intel and AMD. Nvidia is pitching the machines as PCs that can run AI agents and large language models locally, with security sandboxes developed with Microsoft.

Pricing has not been announced. Microsoft's version will be a new Surface Laptop Ultra, and more than 100 software makers, including Adobe and Xbox, have said they will support the platform. Earlier attempts to bring Arm-based chips to Windows computers struggled, so the reception from buyers will be closely watched.

title: Xi Jinping makes rare visit to North Korea and pledges closer ties with Kim
dek: It was the Chinese leader's first trip to Pyongyang in seven years, timed for the 65th anniversary of the two countries' friendship treaty.
body: Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in Pyongyang on 8 June for a state visit and held talks with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. Both sides pledged to deepen cooperation and keep in closer strategic contact. Chinese state media said Mr Xi offered to expand cooperation in trade, farming, construction and technology.

Relations between the neighbours had cooled in recent years, partly because China backed international sanctions over North Korea's nuclear programme, while Pyongyang grew closer to Russia. Analysts said the trip showed Beijing wants to reassert its influence. Mr Kim restated his support for China's position on Taiwan.

North Korean media did not say whether nuclear weapons or relations with the United States were discussed, and denuclearisation did not appear to be on the agenda. The visit came weeks after Mr Xi hosted both US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Beijing.

title: Apple unveils a rebuilt, conversational Siri at its WWDC developer conference
dek: The overhauled assistant, called Siri AI, gets its own app and can carry out multi-step tasks using what is on a user's screen.
body: Apple used the opening keynote of its Worldwide Developers Conference on 8 June to introduce Siri AI, a major rebuild of its voice assistant. It can hold back-and-forth conversations, draw on personal information and what is on screen, and handle tasks with several steps, such as drafting a message using details from emails and calendars. It also has a dedicated app.

Apple has been under pressure to catch up with rivals in generative AI after an earlier promise of a smarter Siri was delayed. The revamp is central to the company's software updates this year, which include iOS 27, and puts Siri on iPhone, Mac and Apple Watch in a more prominent role.

Apple said the new Siri would arrive in beta later in the year. Other features include a new voice, more accurate dictation, and a writing tool in Mail and Messages that adapts drafts to how a user usually writes to each contact. Apple said Siri would also be built more deeply into Spotlight search on the Mac.

title: US forecasters confirm El Niño has arrived and could become very strong
dek: NOAA said the warming of the Pacific is expected to intensify into the northern winter, raising the risk of drought and floods worldwide.
body: The US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration said on 11 June that El Niño conditions are now present in the tropical Pacific and are expected to strengthen into the northern winter of 2026-27. The weather pattern occurs when sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern Pacific stay well above average for months.

El Niño shifts rainfall and temperature patterns around the globe. It often brings drier, hotter weather to parts of Southeast Asia and Australia and heavier rain elsewhere, and it tends to push global temperatures higher. Forecasters said this event could help make the coming period one of the warmest on record.

NOAA put the chance of a very strong El Niño between November and January at 63 per cent, which would place it among the most powerful since records began in 1950. Governments and farmers in Asia are watching closely because past strong events have hurt harvests and raised the risk of haze and water shortages.

title: Mexico beat South Africa 2-0 to open the first 48-team World Cup
dek: The opener at Mexico City's Estadio Azteca featured three red cards and gave Mexico its first win in a World Cup opening game.
body: Co-hosts Mexico began the 2026 World Cup with a 2-0 win over South Africa at the Estadio Azteca on 11 June, in front of more than 80,000 fans. Julián Quiñones scored inside the first nine minutes and Raúl Jiménez headed in the second midway through the second half. The match also saw three players sent off, two from South Africa.

The tournament is the largest in the competition's history, with 48 teams instead of 32, and is being staged across Mexico, the United States and Canada. The Azteca became the first stadium to host matches at three World Cups, having also staged games in 1970 and 1986.

The result ended a long run without success for Mexico in tournament openers, giving the team its first win in eight opening matches. The expanded format means more group games than ever before, with the tournament running until a final in the United States in July.

title: SpaceX shares jump on debut after the largest stock market listing in history
dek: Elon Musk's rocket and satellite company raised about $75 billion and ended its first trading day valued at roughly $2 trillion.
body: SpaceX began trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker SPCX on 12 June after selling about 555.6 million shares at US$135 each, raising roughly US$75 billion. The stock opened at US$150 and closed the day at about US$161, a gain of around 19 per cent from the offer price.

The offering beat the previous record set by Saudi Aramco in 2019, making it the biggest initial public offering ever. It gives ordinary investors their first direct chance to own shares in the company behind Falcon rockets and the Starlink satellite internet service, and it lifted the fortunes of founder Elon Musk.

Trading volume was heavy, and the first-day close put SpaceX's market value at around US$2 trillion. Analysts were split, with some issuing optimistic price targets and at least one research firm recommending investors sell. Nasdaq said the company could become eligible to join the Nasdaq-100 index within weeks.

title: South Korea's former president Yoon Suk Yeol jailed for 30 years over drone flights
dek: A Seoul court found the ex-leader responsible for sending military drones into North Korea in 2024, a case linked to his failed martial law bid.
body: The Seoul Central District Court on 12 June sentenced former South Korean president Yoon Suk Yeol to 30 years in prison over military drone flights into North Korea in October 2024. Pyongyang said the drones dropped propaganda leaflets, and the flights sharply raised tensions on the peninsula. The sentence matched what special prosecutors had asked for.

Prosecutors argued the operation was designed to provoke the North and create a pretext for the martial law declaration Mr Yoon made in December 2024, which quickly collapsed. The ruling adds to his legal troubles: in February a court sentenced him to life in prison for leading an insurrection linked to that declaration.

Mr Yoon denies wrongdoing. His lawyers said he neither ordered nor approved the flights, which they described as a response to months of North Korean balloons carrying rubbish across the border. He remains in custody and can appeal the ruling, as can his former defence minister, who was given the same sentence.

title: US and Iran sign interim deal as American naval blockade is lifted
dek: The memorandum sets out a path to reopen Gulf shipping and opens a window for talks on a final agreement, including Iran's nuclear programme.
body: The United States and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding on 17 June aimed at ending their conflict. A day later, US Central Command said it had lifted the naval blockade of Iranian ports that began on 12 April. During the blockade, 142 commercial ships were turned away and nine vessels that did not comply were disabled.

The deal matters far beyond the region because the Strait of Hormuz is one of the world's most important routes for oil and gas. Disruption there had pushed up energy prices for importers across Asia, including Singapore. Reopening normal shipping is one of the agreement's central aims.

Many questions remain. Reported terms include sanctions relief and a fund to help Iran rebuild, but key issues such as uranium enrichment were left for further talks within about 60 days. US naval ships are staying in the area to monitor compliance, and officials on both sides said a final deal still had to be negotiated.

title: Twin powerful earthquakes strike northern Venezuela, collapsing buildings near Caracas
dek: A magnitude 7.2 quake was followed within a minute by a 7.5 tremor, with the coastal state of La Guaira among the worst-hit areas.
body: Two major earthquakes struck northern Venezuela on 24 June, less than a minute apart. The US Geological Survey measured the first at magnitude 7.2 and the second at 7.5, both centred in Yaracuy state west of Caracas. Buildings collapsed in the capital and in La Guaira, the port area on the Caribbean coast, which officials declared a disaster zone.

The pair of quakes was among the strongest to hit the country in modern times and struck a densely populated region. Acting President Delcy Rodríguez declared a state of emergency. The early count of dozens killed and hundreds injured rose sharply in the following days as rescuers reached more collapsed homes and apartment blocks.

Nearly two dozen aftershocks followed, and experts warned more strong tremors were possible. Field hospitals were set up in La Guaira, and rescue teams from the United States and neighbouring countries arrived to help search the rubble. Officials said damage to homes and infrastructure was widespread.

title: Late-June heatwave smashes temperature records across Europe
dek: Countries from Spain to Poland logged their hottest June days on record, and Western Europe had its warmest June since records began.
body: An intense heatwave in the last week of June broke temperature records across Europe. France had its hottest day on record on 24 June, Spain recorded its hottest June days, and on 28 June Germany reached 41.7°C while Hungary set a new June record. Poland, the Czech Republic and Denmark provisionally set all-time national highs.

The World Meteorological Organization later said Western Europe had its warmest June on record, averaging more than 3°C above the 1991–2020 norm. Scientists link more frequent and severe heatwaves to climate change. The heat put pressure on health services, and several countries reported heat-related deaths.

Dry conditions combined with the heat to raise wildfire activity, especially in Spain, Portugal and southern France, where authorities issued high fire danger warnings. Drought risk also grew in parts of eastern Europe. The WMO said ocean temperatures outside the polar regions reached their highest level on record for June.

title: Trump declares Iran ceasefire over after new US and Iranian attacks
dek: Strikes and counter-strikes followed attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz, putting talks between Washington and Tehran at risk.
body: US President Donald Trump said on July 8 that the ceasefire with Iran was over, speaking at a NATO summit in Ankara. US Central Command said it struck more than 80 targets after Iranian attacks on three ships in the Strait of Hormuz. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said they had hit US military sites in Bahrain and Kuwait.

The truce had followed a memorandum signed weeks earlier that was meant to end the fighting, lift a US naval blockade and reopen the strait. Before the war began in February, about a fifth of the world's daily oil trade passed through Hormuz, so renewed fighting raises risks for energy prices and shipping, including for import-dependent Asian economies.

Trump said US negotiators could keep talking even as he threatened more strikes and a possible return of the naval blockade. The US Treasury also revoked a waiver that had allowed some Iranian crude sales. Gulf states condemned the attacks on Bahrain and Kuwait, and mediators worked in the following days to calm tensions and revive talks.

title: OpenAI launches GPT-5.6 family in three sizes aimed at coding and business
dek: The new Sol, Terra and Luna models arrive across ChatGPT, Codex and the API, alongside a workplace assistant called ChatGPT Work.
body: OpenAI released GPT-5.6 on July 9 as a family of three models. Sol is the flagship, Terra sits in the middle and Luna is the low-cost option. All three are available in ChatGPT, the Codex coding tool and OpenAI's developer API. The company also introduced ChatGPT Work, an assistant for drafting documents, spreadsheets and presentations.

OpenAI is pitching the release at enterprise work, software development and scientific research, areas where it competes most directly with Anthropic. It says Sol is its strongest coding model so far and uses far fewer tokens on coding tasks, which can cut costs for companies running large workloads. It also described GPT-5.6 as its most capable model yet for cybersecurity defence.

API prices range from US$1 per million input tokens for Luna to US$5 for Sol. TechCrunch noted that the Trump administration had earlier sought to restrict the model's rollout over worries about misuse of its cyber abilities. The benchmark claims came from OpenAI, and wider independent testing will show how the models perform in everyday use.

title: Singapore economy grows 5.7% in second quarter on strong AI-driven chip demand
dek: Advance estimates show manufacturing expanded 12.2 per cent from a year earlier, led by electronics and precision engineering.
body: Singapore's economy grew 5.7 per cent year on year in the second quarter of 2026, according to advance estimates released by the Ministry of Trade and Industry on July 14. That was slower than the 6.3 per cent recorded in the first quarter. On a quarter-on-quarter, seasonally adjusted basis, the economy grew 1.1 per cent.

Manufacturing drove the growth, expanding 12.2 per cent from a year earlier. Electronics and precision engineering benefited from strong AI-related demand for semiconductors and chipmaking equipment. Not every industry gained: chemicals output fell because of feedstock disruptions linked to the conflict in the Middle East, and biomedical manufacturing also shrank.

The advance figures are based mainly on April and May data and can be revised. In a later update on August 11, the ministry said growth for the quarter was 5.9 per cent and raised its full-year 2026 forecast to between 4.5 and 5.5 per cent, up from 2 to 4 per cent earlier.

title: Mira Murati's Thinking Machines releases Inkling, its first open-weight AI model
dek: The large model can be downloaded and customised, and is meant as a base for organisations that want AI tuned to their own needs.
body: Thinking Machines Lab, the start-up founded by former OpenAI chief technology officer Mira Murati, released its first in-house model, Inkling, on July 15. It is open-weight, meaning outside developers can download and modify it. The mixture-of-experts model has 975 billion parameters in total, of which about 41 billion are active for any given task.

Inkling was trained on text, images, audio and video, though for now it answers only in text and code. The company openly says it is not the strongest model available, and instead pitches it as a starting point that firms can fine-tune through Tinker, its customisation platform. The approach reflects a bet that tailored models will matter more than one general system.

The release adds to a crowded field of open models, many of them from Chinese labs. Thinking Machines said it used some open models, including Moonshot AI's Kimi K2.5, to generate early training data, and trained Inkling entirely on Nvidia hardware. The company has about 200 staff and earlier previewed research on AI that copes with being interrupted mid-conversation.

title: Databricks valued at US$188 billion in new Coatue-led funding round
dek: The data and AI software company signed a term sheet that lifts its valuation well above the US$134 billion set earlier this year.
body: Databricks said on July 16 that it had signed a term sheet for a strategic funding round valuing the company at US$188 billion, Reuters reported. Existing investor Coatue is leading the round, which includes both new and existing backers. The Wall Street Journal, citing people familiar with the matter, put the size of the round at about US$3 billion.

The jump shows how strongly investors still back firms that help businesses use AI on their own data. Earlier this year Databricks raised about US$5 billion at a US$134 billion valuation, so the new figure marks a rise of roughly 40 per cent within months. The company itself has not said how much the round will raise.

Databricks expects the round to close later in the northern summer. The company sells software that lets organisations store and analyse large amounts of data and build AI tools on top of it. Its rising valuation is being watched as a sign of how much investors are willing to pay for enterprise AI businesses.

title: Japan protests Chinese live-fire drill inside its claimed waters near Okinotori
dek: Beijing rejected the complaint, saying the remote Pacific outcrop is a rock that cannot have an exclusive economic zone.
body: Japan said a Chinese navy destroyer fired machine guns at a floating target during a drill inside Japan's claimed exclusive economic zone near Okinotori on July 19. The Chinese ship was sailing with a Russian vessel as part of a wider joint exercise. Tokyo lodged a protest, saying such activity could endanger ships in the area.

It was the first time Japan had publicly disclosed a Chinese live-fire drill in its economic zone, a sign of worsening ties between the neighbours. China's foreign ministry called the protest unreasonable and said Okinotori is a rock, not an island, so it cannot generate an exclusive economic zone under the UN law of the sea.

Okinotori is a tiny reef roughly halfway between Okinawa and Guam. Japan's claim to the waters around it is not recognised by China, South Korea or Taiwan. Relations between Tokyo and Beijing have been strained since late 2025, when Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said a Taiwan crisis could involve Japan.

title: Spain beat Argentina 1-0 in extra time to win the 2026 World Cup
dek: Substitute Ferran Torres scored the only goal in New Jersey, giving Spain its second men's world title.
body: Spain won the 2026 FIFA World Cup on July 19, beating defending champions Argentina 1-0 after extra time at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey. Substitute Ferran Torres scored in the 106th minute. Argentina played all of extra time with ten men after Enzo Fernandez was sent off for a second yellow card in stoppage time.

It is Spain's second men's World Cup, after its win in 2010, and makes it the first country to hold the men's and women's titles at the same time. Spain conceded only one goal in eight matches, a record for a champion. Coach Luis de la Fuente, 65, became the oldest coach to win the tournament.

The final capped the first World Cup to feature 48 teams, hosted across the United States, Canada and Mexico. Argentina goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez made 12 saves, the most in a World Cup final, as Spain dominated possession and chances. For Lionel Messi, the match was expected to be his last World Cup appearance.

title: EU adopts 21st sanctions package against Russia, targeting shadow fleet and banks
dek: The package adds 41 more vessels to the blacklist and widens restrictions on dozens of financial institutions.
body: The European Union adopted its 21st package of sanctions against Russia on July 23. It adds 41 vessels from Russia's so-called shadow fleet, on top of 632 already listed, and makes 218 new designations of people and organisations. The measures also widen bans on dealings with Russian banks and target several oil refineries.

The shadow fleet refers to tankers that help Russia keep selling oil despite Western price caps. By adding ships and the firms that service them, including refuelling vessels and a crewing agency, the EU aims to cut revenue that funds the war in Ukraine. The package also targets crypto services that could be used to get around sanctions.
